proposals.label: Physical geography
proposals.learning_takeaway: Interactions among water, air, land, and life shape the landscapes physical geographers study.

proposed_parent.note: Physical geography is a branch of geography.

limits: Landscape interactions, not an exhaustive field survey.

proposals.label: Mercator projection
proposals.learning_takeaway: Mercator turns constant compass bearings into straight lines while enlarging areas toward the poles.

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as a map projection.

limits: Rhumb lines need not be shortest routes.

proposals.label: Azimuthal equidistant projection
proposals.learning_takeaway: Distances and directions are accurate from the map’s center, not between every pair of points.

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as a map projection.

limits: Distance guarantee applies from the center.

proposals.label: Latitude
proposals.learning_takeaway: Latitude measures north–south angular position from the equator, with poles at ninety degrees.

proposed_parent.note: Latitude specifies a geographic coordinate component.

limits: Geographic coordinate meaning.

proposals.label: Longitude
proposals.learning_takeaway: Longitude measures east–west position from a chosen prime meridian; equal degree steps cover less distance near the poles.

proposed_parent.note: Longitude specifies a geographic coordinate component.

limits: Prime meridian must be specified.

proposals.label: Geographic coordinate system
proposals.learning_takeaway: Coordinates need a reference model as well as latitude and longitude to specify Earth locations.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: A datum alone is insufficient.

proposals.label: Isthmus of Panama
proposals.learning_takeaway: Panama’s land bridge joined the Americas while separating marine populations and changing ocean circulation.
limits: No disputed exact closure date asserted.

proposals.label: Plitvice Lakes National Park
proposals.learning_takeaway: Calcium carbonate deposits build natural barriers that continually reshape this Croatian lake system.
limits: Tufa-building process is the selected angle.

proposals.label: Primary source
proposals.learning_takeaway: Firsthand records connect us to past participants, but their perspectives and biases still require interpretation.

proposed_parent.note: Firsthand records are materials of historical inquiry.

limits: Primary does not mean unbiased.

proposals.label: Public history
proposals.learning_takeaway: Public historians work with communities to interpret the past in museums, archives, and other public settings.

proposed_parent.note: Public history interprets the past with publics.

limits: Collaboration varies across settings.

proposals.label: Archive
proposals.learning_takeaway: Archives select records of lasting value, preserve them, and make documentary evidence available for future use.

discovery_evidence.locator: Organization definition and Work of Archivists; lines 247–261

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Archive also names records and buildings.

proposals.label: Great Migration (African American)
proposals.learning_takeaway: Black migration out of the South combined flight from racial oppression with pursuit of work and education.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Destination discrimination also persisted.

proposals.label: Underground Railroad
proposals.learning_takeaway: Freedom seekers escaped slavery through many routes, sometimes unaided and sometimes assisted by organized or spontaneous help.
proposals.identity_reason: Self-emancipation effort, not a literal railway.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: No single organization or uniform route.

proposals.label: Treaty of Waitangi
proposals.learning_takeaway: Differences between the Māori and English texts shaped disputes over governance and chiefly authority.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Translations conveyed different understandings of authority.

proposals.label: Treaty of Tordesillas
proposals.learning_takeaway: Spain and Portugal drew an Atlantic dividing line for imperial claims, placing eastern Brazil in Portugal’s sphere.

discovery_evidence.locator: French nomination, PDF page 1 (index 0), summary lines 6–14; page 4 (index 3), lines 111–117

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Imperial claims do not establish Indigenous consent.

proposals.label: Berlin Wall
proposals.learning_takeaway: The wall enclosed West Berlin to stop flight from East Germany and grew into a layered border system.

discovery_evidence.locator: Index and Building the Wall in August 1961; lines 36–41

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Not merely a single concrete wall.

proposals.label: Treaty of Paris (1783)
proposals.learning_takeaway: Britain recognized US independence in the peace settlement, which also defined boundaries for the new country.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Distinct from other treaties of Paris.

proposals.label: Sonnet
proposals.learning_takeaway: Traditional sonnets compress thought into fourteen lines, often using a turn to redirect the argument.

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as a poetic form.

limits: Traditional pattern allows later variations.

proposals.label: Haiku
proposals.learning_takeaway: Haiku evokes a brief moment through concentrated images; modern adaptations need not follow a fixed syllable count.

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as a poetic form.

limits: Modern adaptations need not use fixed counts.

proposals.label: Irony
proposals.learning_takeaway: Irony creates gaps between appearance and reality, such as a character’s ignorance of information readers already know.

proposed_parent.note: Presented as a literary device.

limits: Dramatic irony is one example.

proposals.label: Motif (narrative)
proposals.learning_takeaway: Repeated details can connect scenes and reinforce themes without being the theme themselves.

proposed_parent.note: Repeated patterns operate within narratives.

limits: A motif is not the theme.

proposals.label: Plot (narrative)
proposals.learning_takeaway: Plot orders actions and their consequences into a structure that makes events feel connected.

proposed_parent.note: Plot arranges a narrative’s events.

limits: One plotting formula is not universal.

proposals.label: First-person narrative
proposals.learning_takeaway: First-person narrators reveal themselves through how they tell events, as well as through what happens.

discovery_evidence.locator: Transcript, first person and direct address; lines 54–65

proposed_parent.note: Point of view shapes narrative telling.

limits: First-person voice; not exhaustive narrator taxonomy.

proposals.label: Fable
proposals.learning_takeaway: Animal stories can dramatize human behavior, as the fox dismisses grapes he cannot reach.
proposals.identity_reason: Moral story genre, illustrated by Aesop.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: One primary story illustrates the genre.

proposals.label: Epic of Sundiata
proposals.learning_takeaway: Sundiata’s epic preserves Mali’s founding story through griots, whose performances connect listeners with ancestral memory.

discovery_evidence.locator: Curriculum Unit 09.01.07, Sundiata discussion, PDF page 6 (index 5); lines 193–219

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Multiple versions; Niane’s recording is one example.

proposals.label: Musicology
proposals.learning_takeaway: Musicology investigates how music is made, understood, and used across societies and historical periods.

discovery_evidence.locator: Opening explanation and Topic Areas; lines 158–175

proposed_parent.note: Musicology is scholarly study of music.

limits: Not restricted to European art music.

proposals.label: Dynamics (music)
proposals.learning_takeaway: Dynamic markings guide loudness; a crescendo asks performers to grow louder.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Open Music Theory notation chapter.

limits: Examples from Western staff notation.

proposals.label: Cadence
proposals.learning_takeaway: A cadence coordinates musical motion into a point of arrival that punctuates a phrase or larger unit.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Open Music Theory form lesson.

limits: Classical tonal context.

proposals.label: Timbre
proposals.learning_takeaway: Different instruments can play the same pitch yet sound distinct because their sound waves have different shapes.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Wave shape is one explanatory angle.

proposals.label: Fugue
proposals.learning_takeaway: A fugue introduces its main theme in successive independent voices, building an imitative texture.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Open Music Theory counterpoint chapter.

limits: High Baroque exposition; later forms vary.

proposals.label: Twelve-tone technique
proposals.learning_takeaway: Twelve-tone composition organizes all twelve pitch classes into ordered rows that can be transformed.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Open Music Theory composition lesson.

limits: Serialism also includes other methods.

proposals.label: Nonchord tone
proposals.learning_takeaway: Notes outside the current chord can connect chord tones; passing tones move by step through the gap.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Music Theory harmony chapter.

limits: Passing tone is one type.

proposals.label: Tritone
proposals.learning_takeaway: In equal temperament, a tritone spans six semitones and can be spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth.
proposals.identity_reason: Musical interval, not a three-note chord.

discovery_evidence.locator: Diminished fifth and augmented fourth, lines 1147, 1236; semitone table, lines 1245–1258

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Open Music Theory interval chapter.

limits: Equal-temperament measurement.

proposals.label: ontology
proposals.learning_takeaway: Ontology asks what exists and how to settle disputed cases such as numbers or properties.

discovery_evidence.locator: What exists and disputed cases, lines 116–119; conceptions of ontology, lines 129–139

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Not a computing ontology.

proposals.label: Problem of induction
proposals.learning_takeaway: Past regularities support predictions, but justifying the jump to unobserved cases risks circular reasoning.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Does not declare prediction useless.

proposals.label: Fallibilism
proposals.learning_takeaway: A belief can be justified without its justification guaranteeing that it is true.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Compatible with some accounts of knowledge.

proposals.label: Categorical imperative
proposals.learning_takeaway: Kant’s universal-law formulation tests whether your action’s guiding rule could be consistently willed for everyone.

discovery_evidence.locator: Section 5, universal-law formulation, lines 132–134; lying-promise example, line 143

proposed_parent.note: A moral principle in Kant’s ethics.

limits: One formulation, not Kant’s whole ethics.

proposals.label: Act utilitarianism
proposals.learning_takeaway: Act utilitarianism evaluates each available action by the overall well-being it would produce.

discovery_evidence.locator: Act/rule contrast, lines 90–93; rules and exceptions, lines 146, 159–162

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly distinguished form of utilitarianism.

limits: Compare available actions.

proposals.label: Rule utilitarianism
proposals.learning_takeaway: Rule utilitarianism evaluates actions through rules whose general acceptance produces the most well-being.

discovery_evidence.locator: Act/rule contrast, lines 90–93; rules and exceptions, lines 146, 159–162

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly distinguished form of utilitarianism.

limits: Rule codes can allow exceptions.

proposals.label: Zeno's paradoxes
proposals.learning_takeaway: One paradox challenges motion because reaching a goal seems to require completing infinitely many halfway steps.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Dichotomy is one paradox, not a proof motion fails.

proposals.label: metaethics
proposals.learning_takeaway: Metaethics asks what moral judgments mean and whether or how they can be true.
proposals.identity_reason: Foundations and status of moral judgment.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Not a list of practical moral rules.

proposals.label: Due process
proposals.learning_takeaway: US due process requires fair procedures when government deprives people of protected life, liberty, or property.

discovery_evidence.locator: What is due process? and promise of fair procedure; lines 6–7, 21–22

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US example; requirements depend on context.

proposals.label: Judicial review
proposals.learning_takeaway: US courts use judicial review to invalidate government actions that conflict with the Constitution.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US example; institutional arrangements vary.

proposals.label: Separation of powers
proposals.learning_takeaway: Separating legislative, executive, and judicial functions lets institutions check one another’s power.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US example; not every system has identical branches.

proposals.label: Federalism
proposals.learning_takeaway: Federalism distributes governing authority between national and regional governments, with some powers shared.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US example; divisions vary.

proposals.label: Ex post facto law
proposals.learning_takeaway: In US law, ex post facto bans prevent retroactive criminal punishment or later increases in punishment.

discovery_evidence.locator: Definition and What Constitutes Punishment; lines 6–14

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US constitutional ban, not every retroactive law.

proposals.label: Grand jury
proposals.learning_takeaway: In US federal courts, grand juries decide whether evidence supports criminal charges, rather than deciding guilt.

discovery_evidence.locator: Trial jury, lines 571–577; grand jury, line 583

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US federal context.

proposals.label: Petit jury
proposals.learning_takeaway: In US federal trials, petit juries decide verdicts, using different proof standards in criminal and civil cases.

discovery_evidence.locator: Trial jury, lines 571–577; grand jury, line 583

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: US federal context.

proposals.label: Bill of Rights 1689
proposals.learning_takeaway: England’s 1689 settlement required Parliament’s agreement for taxation and protected speech within Parliament.

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: Parliamentary speech; not the US Bill of Rights.

proposals.label: Zakat
proposals.learning_takeaway: Zakat gives part of accumulated wealth to those in need and is understood as purification of the remaining wealth.

proposed_parent.note: Identified as an Islamic practice.

limits: No universal threshold or rate asserted.

proposals.label: Shahada
proposals.learning_takeaway: The Muslim profession of faith joins belief in God’s oneness with recognition of Muhammad as God’s messenger.

proposed_parent.note: Identified as an Islamic declaration.

limits: Two linked affirmations, not a full theology.

proposals.label: Baptism
proposals.learning_takeaway: Baptism marks entry into a Christian community through water; traditions differ over age and method.

proposed_parent.note: Identified as Christian initiation.

limits: Some traditions do not practice outward baptism.

proposals.label: Eucharist
proposals.learning_takeaway: The Eucharist gathers Christians around shared sacred bread and wine.
proposals.identity_reason: Eucharistic rite, not church-family meaning of communion.

proposed_parent.note: Identified as a Christian rite.

limits: No single denominational account asserted.

proposals.label: Mandala
proposals.learning_takeaway: In Esoteric Buddhism, cosmic diagrams guide meditation alongside hand gestures and sacred formulas.
proposals.identity_reason: Sacred diagram, not a decorative pattern alone.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Esoteric Buddhist use of mandalas.

limits: One Buddhist use; other traditions also use mandalas.

proposals.label: Moksha
proposals.learning_takeaway: Vedanta describes moksha as liberation from rebirth through insight, while its schools disagree about self and ultimate reality.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Vedanta context for liberation.

limits: Vedanta example; Hindu accounts differ.

proposals.label: nirvana
proposals.learning_takeaway: In Buddhism, nirvana involves extinguishing greed, hatred, and delusion that fuel rebirth.

proposed_parent.note: Explicit Buddhist meaning of nirvana.

limits: Buddhist usage selected; other senses unaddressed.

proposals.label: Kumbh Mela
proposals.learning_takeaway: Pilgrims gather at rotating Indian river sites for sacred bathing and the transmission of religious traditions.

proposed_parent.note: Identified as Hindu pilgrimage gathering.

limits: Purification is a religious belief.

proposals.label: Stained glass
proposals.learning_takeaway: Lead strips join colored glass pieces into window images, while painted details can supply outlines and shadows.
proposals.identity_reason: Colored glass used for pictorial windows.

discovery_evidence.locator: Colored glass, painted details, and lead assembly, lines 109–113

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as stained-glass art.

limits: Medieval European construction example.

proposals.label: Mosaic
proposals.learning_takeaway: Small pieces of stone, ceramic, or glass can form durable images, as Roman floor mosaics demonstrate.
proposals.identity_reason: Art made from assembled small pieces.

discovery_evidence.locator: Floor durability and tesserae, lines 111–119; color materials, lines 131–132

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly discussed as an art form.

limits: Roman floors are one example.

proposals.label: Gouache
proposals.learning_takeaway: Gouache’s opaque, matte paint can supply bright highlights within otherwise transparent watercolor compositions.

discovery_evidence.locator: Transparent medium and white support, lines 7–23; opaque gouache and highlights, lines 42–47

proposed_parent.note: Editorial grouping from the inspected subject.

limits: One use within watercolor compositions.

proposals.label: Color field
proposals.learning_takeaway: Large color areas can contain subtle shades; Rothko achieved this through layers of thinned paint.
proposals.identity_reason: Color Field painting, not a literal field.

discovery_evidence.locator: Transcript: blocks and shades, lines 9–10; layered thin paint, lines 12–14

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as Color Field paintings.

limits: Rothko’s process illustrates one approach.

proposals.label: Still life
proposals.learning_takeaway: Arrangements of ordinary objects can suggest mortality or wealth, as Dutch still lifes show through skulls, watches, and luxuries.

discovery_evidence.locator: Objects, mortality symbolism, and luxury, lines 132–144

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as a painting genre.

limits: Northern European examples; meanings are not universal.

proposals.label: Pointillism
proposals.learning_takeaway: Small dots of separate colors can blend visually at a distance, as in Seurat’s mature technique.

discovery_evidence.locator: Object explanation, lines 10–11; audio transcript, lines 68–71

proposed_parent.note: Painting technique illustrated through Seurat.

limits: Final painting, not the study’s broader patches.

proposals.label: Ukiyo-e
proposals.learning_takeaway: Commercial ukiyo-e prints depended on coordinated work by designers, carvers, printers, and publishers.

discovery_evidence.locator: Commercial production and four specialists, lines 100–104

proposed_parent.note: Explicit ukiyo-e woodblock print production.

limits: Print production is one facet; paintings also exist.

proposals.label: Genre painting
proposals.learning_takeaway: Scenes of ordinary life can carry social commentary, even when their subjects appear familiar.

discovery_evidence.locator: Everyday subjects and moral/social commentary, lines 209, 215–216, 231

proposed_parent.note: Explicitly identified as a painting genre.

limits: Northern European examples; not all scenes moralize.
